AUTOMATION OF TEST TASK GENERATION WITH A SPECIFIED DIFFICULTY LEVEL BASED ON NEURAL NETWORK MODELS
recent_literature.abstract: <jats:p>This article presents a study of methods for automatically generating test items with a controlled level of complexity based on neural network models. The aim of the study is to comparatively analyze the effectiveness of various architectural approaches to generating multiple-choice questions and assessing their complexity using Bloom’s taxonomy. Using an experimental database including publicly available datasets, the potential of modern neural network approaches for automating the development of assessment materials in education is demonstrated. The results of computational experiments show that the two-stage Generator-Critic architecture using fine-tuned T5 and a RuBERT-based classifier achieves the best quality indicators (BLEU-4 = 34,2, ROUGE-L = 61,5 %, complexity classification accuracy = 92,8 %), but requires significant computational resources. The hybrid CNN-BiLSTM architecture for complexity classification demonstrates an optimal balance between quality (F1-score = 88,4 %) and speed (≈ 0.04 s per sample), making it preferable for integration into mass testing systems. Of particular scientific significance is the analysis of the «semantic drift effect»: when generating questions based on unfamiliar domain models, quality drops by 12-18 %, indicating the need for domain adaptation methods. Practical recommendations for integrating test generation systems into the educational process have been developed, including the use of expert validation of generated questions and explainable AI methods to increase the trust in automatically generated test materials. The practical significance of this research lies in the development of a methodology for selecting the optimal architecture based on available computing resources and the quality requirements for generated test items. Furthermore, the article substantiates the need for regular adaptation of models to new subject areas to reduce semantic drift and proposes an approach for expert post-validation of generated items. The obtained results form the basis for the development of adaptive test generation systems integrated into digital educational platforms.</jats:p>

recent_literature.title: Uncertainty-Aware Text-Conditioned Diffusion for Robust Vibration Synthesis under Domain Shifts
recent_literature.abstract: <jats:p>Recent advances in generative AI enable high-fidelity synthesis, but reliability under domain shifts and low-SNR conditions in engineering vibration remains underexplored. We present Uncertainty-Aware Text-to-Vibration Diffusion (U-T2V), a text-conditioned framework that models and calibrates uncertainty to deliver risk-aware vibration synthesis for predictive maintenance. Natural-language descriptions of machine configuration, operating regime, and fault semantics are encoded as global conditions for a heteroscedastic diffusion backbone that predicts both mean and variance, capturing data (aleatoric) uncertainty. Multi-sample inference (or lightweight ensembles) estimates model (epistemic) uncertainty, and a risk-aware sampler adapts the temperature schedule to suppress high-uncertainty trajectories. Post-hoc calibration (temperature scaling or Dirichlet-style calibration) aligns model confidence with empirical coverage, enabling calibrated prediction intervals for fault-relevant spectral primitives such as BPFI/BPFO bands. Evaluated on CWRU, XJTU-SY, and a lab-scale rig under controlled domain shifts in speed, load, and sensor placement, U-T2V matches or exceeds baseline fidelity (FVD, WS, SD) while markedly improving reliability—lower ECE and NLL, higher OOD-AUROC, and accurate coverage with compact intervals. In downstream diagnosis, uncertainty-filtered augmentation consistently improves robustness with limited labels. U-T2V advances calibrated, risk-aware generative vibration synthesis for trustworthy augmentation and simulation in condition monitoring.</jats:p>

recent_literature.title: Task-Conditioned Early Prediction of Navigation Failure in Information Architecture Evaluation
Neuro-Symbolic Task Planning for Tabletop Manipulation under Perceptual Uncertainty
recent_literature.abstract: <jats:p>Robotic manipulation in unstructured environments requires reliable symbolic reasoning from noisy perceptual input, yet existing neuro-symbolic systems treat perception as a deterministic oracle and cannot quantify or act on prediction uncertainty. We present a neuro-symbolic framework for tabletop manipulation that explicitly propagates uncertainty from visual perception to symbolic task planning. A hybrid Transformer-GNN architecture extracts probabilistic symbolic states (spatial predicates with calibrated confidence scores) from RGB-D observations, and an uncertainty-aware PDDL planner actively triggers information-gathering actions (look\_closer, push\_obstacle) when predicate confidence falls below a learned threshold. Evaluated on 10,047 PyBullet-simulated scenes (3--10 objects, Franka and UR5 platforms), the system achieves 94\%/90\%/88\% task success on Simple Stack, Deep Stack, and Clear+Stack benchmarks (90.7\% average), outperforming the strongest POMDP baseline by 10--14 percentage points while reducing planning time from 100+\,ms to under 15\,ms. A Markov Random Field analysis of predicate dependencies yields tighter uncertainty bounds than independence-based approaches, and a convergence theorem explicitly links calibration quality to planning guarantees---validated empirically within 17\% of theoretical predictions. The framework provides interpretable, uncertainty-aware plans suitable for deployment on autonomous robotic systems operating under real-world perceptual conditions.</jats:p>

Catatonia recovery separates two intervention axes that constrain electroconvulsive therapy
recent_literature.abstract: Catatonia recovers through capacities returning in a fixed dependency order, and benzodiazepines and electroconvulsive therapy work without a known target. On an evidence-coupled bistable cascade over that order we take three quantities to be externally accessible: the root capacity, the coupling between capacities, and accumulated evidence. Here we show that evidence has no external port and the other two act on disjoint regions. While every capacity is below threshold, a maximum principle forbids non-negative diffusive coupling, on any graph and either direction, from crossing the switching surface, so acute conversion needs an excursion, whereas an additive excitatory drive converts on its own. Above one exact criterion, the prevailing threshold squared over four, propagation separates into immediate, metastable and confined. On the modelled branch coupling alone shifts the resting first stage, so a treatment effective in both states is predicted to have separable excursion and coupling components, identifiable in model coordinates.

Interpretability Without Full Recoverability: Formal Identifiability, Synthetic Recovery, and Reportability of Withdrawal-Side Parameters in the Continuous Moral-Social World Model
recent_literature.abstract: <jats:p>Mechanistically specified models are often treated as interpretable because each coefficient has an assigned role in the equations. That semantic assignment is necessary but not sufficient for inference: parameter interpretation also requires structural identifiability of the parameter-to-observation map and practical recovery under finite, noisy data. We formalize this distinction for the Continuous Moral-Social World Model (CMS-WM), a simulator with phenotype-state, world-state, and action-policy modules. The revised analysis makes the complete withdrawal-side policy explicit, defines the observation operator, proves exact softmax scaling and common-shift invariances, and evaluates effective withdrawal parameters in reproducible synthetic recovery experiments. In a principal batch of 30 ground-truth settings with 1,000 trials each, the ambiguity-linked coupling showed moderate rank recovery (Spearman rho = 0.52; median normalized absolute error = 0.19), whereas the friction-linked coupling was weak under correlated inputs (rho = 0.21; median error = 0.34). When friction was experimentally orthogonalized from ambiguity, friction recovery improved (rho = 0.68; median error = 0.087), demonstrating configuration-dependent rather than intrinsic interpretability. Pressure coupling and the withdrawal threshold remained insufficiently rank-recoverable in the principal design (rho = 0.37 and 0.30, respectively), despite substantial threshold activation. In contrast, out-of-sample action-regime prediction was stable: dominant-regime agreement was 100%, median predictive L1 distance was 0.0187, and median Jensen-Shannon divergence was 7.2 x 10^-5. These findings support a hierarchical reportability framework: regime-level behavior is reportable; the ambiguity-linked parameter is cautiously reportable; friction is design-conditional; and pressure coupling and threshold should not receive substantive mechanistic interpretation under the present observation model. The study is an internal synthetic verification of the model-observation pairing, not external validation of psychopathy or antisocial behavior.</jats:p>

recent_literature.title: From Predictive State to Viable Action: Action Sufficiency, Safe Diagnosis, and the Operational Recoverability Bound
recent_literature.abstract: <jats:p>A predictive state retains every distinction from history that can alter a declared future law. A living controller, clinician, robot, or certified AI system often needs a coarser object: enough information to choose an acceptable action. Let A_alpha(s) be the actions with success probability at least 1-alpha from state s. A deterministic code is action-sufficient if and only if every code cell has a nonempty common-action intersection. For finite, individually feasible state and action sets, minimum code size is exactly the chromatic number of the hypergraph of inclusion-minimal empty intersections, equivalently the minimum number of actions whose success sets cover all states. Pairwise conflicts give only a lower bound. This static selection result does not establish that the code is recursively updateable or is a sufficient internal state for a sequential controller. Recovery under partial observation adds diagnostic time, safety, and action availability. For two equiprobable hidden states with disjoint acceptable-action sets, the minimum probability of selecting an unacceptable action after a fixed, non-disturbing diagnostic is (1-TV(P_1,P_2))/2. A selection-error tolerance delta therefore requires TV(P_1,P_2) &gt;= 1-2 delta. This is not in general a lower bound on biological failure; action outcome risks require separate accounting. We supply that distinction, a robust policy definition of operational recoverability, and finite reproducible checks. The contribution is a biological and experimental synthesis of predictive representations, state abstraction, set cover, viability, and safe diagnosis. Its empirical claim is that measured hidden-state distinctions can improve held-out action selection before a rescue window closes; no biological dataset or clinical efficacy result is established here.</jats:p>

Fine-Tuning Multimodal Large Language Models: From Parameter Updates to Data-Centric, Modality-Aware Adaptation
recent_literature.abstract: <jats:p>Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have moved from tightly coupled vision-language systems toward general-purpose models that ingest and reason over mixtures of images, video, audio, documents, and text. Fine-tuning is the main mechanism for converting broad pretrained competence into reliable behavior for a target domain, interaction pattern, or modality, yet the adaptation problem is substantially harder than text-only language-model fine-tuning. MLLMs contain heterogeneous components with different failure modes: modality encoders can lose pretrained invariances, modality connectors can bottleneck information, and the language backbone can absorb both useful domain knowledge and harmful task-specific shortcuts. This white paper surveys the design space of MLLM fine-tuning, synthesizing classical transfer learning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, multimodal instruction tuning, preference optimization, continual adaptation, and systems efficiency. It advances a position that the unit of adaptation should not be treated as the model's parameter vector alone. Instead, effective fine-tuning should be organized around four coupled objects: the data distribution, the adaptation locus, the crossmodal interface, and the deployment constraint. We review full fine-tuning, adapters, prompt and prefix tuning, selective tuning, LoRA and its variants, quantized fine-tuning, projector-only updates, sparse expert routing, and hybrid strategies; then connect these methods to multimodal data construction, synthetic instruction generation, grounding and hallucination control, personalization, safety, and evaluation. We argue that the most promising future direction is modality-aware, sparsely activated, data-centric adaptation: train only the parameters that are causally relevant to the required capability, preserve pretrained structure wherever possible, explicitly supervise cross-modal grounding, and evaluate both task gains and retained generality. The paper concludes with practical recommendations and a research agenda for developing MLLMs that are adaptable without becoming brittle, expensive, or ungrounded.</jats:p>
